summary: Describes using the SEED block cipher in SRTP for confidentiality of RTP traffic and RTCP control traffic.

eli5.summary: SEED is a secret code. This explains how to use it to scramble audio and video calls so strangers can't listen in.

subtitle: How to use the Korean SEED block cipher to encrypt and authenticate secure voice and video streams.

tldr.problem: SRTP protects real-time media, but it was specified around AES, so users of the SEED cipher, which is widely used in South Korea, had no standard way to use it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines SEED in counter mode (SEED-CTR) with HMAC-SHA1 as the mandatory transform, optional SEED-CCM and SEED-GCM modes, a nonce format for those modes, and key derivation using SEED in counter mode.
tldr.outcome: Three SRTP crypto suites were registered so SDP can signal SEED. It is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted.

today: RFC 5669 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of SEED in SRTP.

sections.title: Introduction to SEED in SRTP
sections.content:
This RFC describes how to use the SEED block cipher inside the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP, RFC 3711) to give confidentiality to RTP media traffic and to RTCP control traffic.

SEED is a symmetric cipher developed by the Korea Information Security Agency (KISA) and a group of experts, beginning in 1998. Its block size and key length are both 128 bits, and it has a 16-round Feistel structure. The RFC says it suits resource-limited settings such as mobile devices and smart cards, and that it is widely used in South Korea for electronic commerce and financial services. The algorithm itself is specified in RFC 4269.
sections.eli5: SEED is a lock that was made in Korea. This document shows how to fit that lock onto the secure call system.

sections.title: The Three SEED Modes
sections.content:
SEED has no restrictions on modes of operation. The RFC defines three.

  • SEED-CTR: counter mode, defined like AES-CM in RFC 3711 with SEED as the block cipher. It MUST be used only together with an authentication function. The default is HMAC-SHA1 with a 160-bit session-authentication key and an 80-bit tag.
  • SEED-CCM: SEED with Counter with CBC-MAC (RFC 3610), which authenticates and encrypts in one step. The tag size M should be the full 80 bits (10 octets), and L is 3, so the nonce is 12 octets. Authentication is done on the plaintext rather than the ciphertext. All SRTP packets MUST be authenticated and encrypted; for SRTCP, encryption is optional but authentication is mandatory.
  • SEED-GCM: SEED with Galois/Counter Mode, using the same four inputs (key, plaintext, nonce, additional authenticated data) and a 12-octet (96-bit) tag.

For CCM and GCM the RTP header is the additional authenticated data and the payload is the plaintext. SEED only supports a 128-bit key.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to run the lock. One just scrambles, and needs a separate seal. The other two scramble and seal at once.

sections.title: Nonce Format for CCM and GCM
sections.content:
CCM and GCM need a 12-octet nonce, a value that must not repeat for the same key. For SRTP it is built from the packet's own fields and a secret salt:

Nonce = (16 bits of zeroes || SSRC || ROC || SEQ) XOR Salt

The 4-octet SSRC and 2-octet sequence number come from the RTP header. The 4-octet rollover counter (ROC) comes from the cryptographic context. The 12-octet salt is produced by the SRTP key derivation function.

For SRTCP the nonce is (16 bits of zeroes || SSRC || 16 bits of zeroes || SRTCP index) XOR Salt, where the SSRC is taken from the RTCP header and the 31-bit SRTCP index is packed zero-filled and right-justified into 4 octets.
sections.eli5: Each packet gets a one-time number made from its own label and a secret, so the lock never uses the same number twice.

sections.title: Key Derivation with SEED-CTR
sections.content:
SRTP derives its session keys from a master key with a pseudo-random function (PRF). RFC 3711 defines this using AES in counter mode. The SEED-CTR PRF is defined the same way, with each AES call replaced by a SEED call.

The PRF is keyed by the 128-bit master key, has an input block size of 128, and can produce n-bit outputs for n up to 2^23. It is SEED in counter mode applied to the master key, with an IV equal to (x*2^16), and the output keystream is cut to the first n bits.
sections.eli5: One master key is stirred by the same machine to produce lots of fresh working keys.

sections.title: Mandatory-to-Implement Transforms
sections.content:
An RTP implementation that supports SEED MUST implement the modes in the RFC's Table 1. This table does not replace the similar table in Section 5 of RFC 3711.

SEED-CTR is mandatory for encryption and for key derivation, and HMAC-SHA1 is mandatory for message integrity. SEED-CCM and SEED-GCM are optional for both encryption and integrity.
sections.eli5: Anyone offering SEED must at least support the basic scramble-plus-seal combination. The fancier combined modes are extras.

sections.title: Security and Registered Crypto Suites
sections.content:
The RFC states that no security problem has been found on SEED, that it is secure against all known attacks including differential cryptanalysis, linear cryptanalysis and related key attacks, and that the best known attack is exhaustive key search. It points readers to the KISA self evaluation report. The security considerations of RFC 3610 and of the GCM specification apply to those modes, and the procedures of RFC 3711 ensure that counter values are not reused.

For signaling, IANA registered three crypto suites for SDP Security Descriptions (RFC 4568): SEED_CTR_128_HMAC_SHA1_80, SEED_128_CCM_80 and SEED_128_GCM_96. The appendix gives test vectors for all three modes.
sections.eli5: The makers say nobody has found a way to crack it except trying every key. Names for the three modes were registered so call setup can pick one.
